paragraphs.text: Neurodevelopmental disorder with or without macrocephaly (NEDMAC) is an X-linked disorder caused by SMARCA1 variants. Its severity varies widely. Features include mild to severe intellectual disability or developmental delay, delayed or regressive speech development, autism spectrum disorder (ASD) features, facial dysmorphism, and other variable features. About half of affected individuals have macrocephaly or brain overgrowth, and it is more common in those with truncating variants. Most affected individuals are hemizygous males with maternally inherited variants. Heterozygous females can also be affected and often have a milder phenotype (Mirzaa et al., 2025; Nishimura et al., 2025).

paragraphs.text: Mirzaa et al. (2025) first studied a large 6-generation family in which 4 individuals had mild to severe intellectual disability or developmental delay and brain overgrowth. The proband, a 12-year-4-month-old boy, had an OFC of +6 SD, no language, severe intellectual disability, and ASD. He also had hydrocephalus that required shunting, hepatosplenomegaly, and overgrowth, with height and weight at +5 SD. His 8-year-old brother had an OFC of +4.3 SD, speech delay, and mild intellectual disability. The brother also had hydrocephalus that did not require shunting, splenomegaly, and overgrowth (height +3 SD, weight +3.7 SD). Their maternal cousins had mild learning disability and normal brain MRI. One cousin, a 14-year-7-month-old girl, had an OFC of +4.9 SD and severe obesity (BMI 50 kg/m2). The other, an 8-year-9-month-old boy, had an OFC of +5.5 SD and obesity. The two carrier mothers, aged 45 and 49 years, had no reported learning disability and only mildly increased head circumference (+1 SD and +1.5 SD).

paragraphs.text: Mirzaa et al. (2025) then reported a total of 35 individuals from 26 families: 26 males and 9 females, aged 2 to 49 years at their last assessment. Most had intellectual disability or developmental delay (27 of 35, 77%) and speech delay and/or speech regression (29 of 35, 83%). In 4 individuals, speech regression was noted rather than delay. Seventeen of 35 individuals (49%) had increased head circumference (OFC at or above +2 SD) and/or reported macrocephaly or brain overgrowth. Increased height (at or above +2 SD) was reported less often (29%), which the authors argued was against a generalized overgrowth syndrome. Other common features were: - motor delay (20 of 34, 59%) - hypotonia (15 of 35, 42%) - seizures or epilepsy (8 of 35, 23%) - behavioral difficulties such as ASD, ADHD, and aggression (19 of 35, 54%); 11 of 35 (31%) were diagnosed with ASD, and in some instances (9 of 25) the behavioral difficulties were linked to regression in speech and mental development Nineteen of 35 individuals had dysmorphic facial features, but the clinical descriptions varied. The recurrent features included: - ear anomalies (11 individuals) - micrognathia (5) - slanted palpebral fissures (5) - prominent forehead (4) - anteverted nostrils (4) - bulbous nasal tip (3) In photographs of 7 affected individuals, relatively common features were frontal bossing, a long face, slanted palpebral fissures, a flat nasal root with a short bulbous nose, anteverted nares, and a thin upper lip. Other recurring findings involved the urogenital tract or kidney (9 individuals), the gastrointestinal tract (9), and the eyes or vision (8); 3 individuals had hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Affected females often had a milder phenotype.

The figure legend of the same report described this change as a homozygous stop-gain variant.

paragraphs.text: Mirzaa et al. (2025) performed exome sequencing in a 6-generation family with intellectual disability or developmental delay and brain overgrowth. They identified a SMARCA1 nonsense variant (R91X) in the proband, his brother, and 2 maternal cousins. The mothers of the affected individuals were heterozygous for the variant, and the paternal grandfather and a maternal uncle did not carry it. Through the MatchMaker Exchange network and other routes, the authors ascertained 25 more families. The total came to 35 individuals with apparently non-mosaic hemizygous or heterozygous SMARCA1 variants, identified by trio exome sequencing in 23 families and genome sequencing in 3. There were 25 unique variants; a second, unrelated family carried the same variant as the index family. The variants comprised 7 nonsense, 3 frameshift, and 15 missense changes. All were predicted to be deleterious, and all were absent or very rare in gnomAD. Sixteen of the 25 variants were located in the ATPase domain (12) or the HSS domain (4). The authors also identified SMARCA1 variants in 7 further families that they judged likely non-causative or non-explanatory. These included a recurrent V384M variant found in 3 families. This variant had previously been reported in a family with schizophrenia, and it was present in gnomAD in 16 alleles, including 7 hemizygotes.

paragraphs.text: Mirzaa et al. (2025) found that Smarca1 knockout mice lacked detectable Smarca1 protein, were viable, and had no obvious gross developmental defects. Brain size showed only slight reductions, in total brain width, corpus callosum length, and the area of the dentate gyrus granule cell layer. Neocortical progenitors and cortical lamination were normal. In behavioral testing, the knockout mice were more active in the dark cycle but otherwise did not differ from controls. In knockout cerebellum, Smarca5 coimmunoprecipitated with Cecr2, which suggested functional compensation for the loss of Smarca1. By contrast, mice with an in-frame deletion of Smarca1 exon 6 (Smarca1ex6del) had a total brain area 10% larger than controls. This enlargement was reduced when the mice were combined with Smarca5 ablation. None of the double mutants (Smarca1/Smarca5, Smarca5/Smarca1ex6del, or Smarca5/Bptf) had a more severe phenotype than Bptf mutants alone.

paragraphs.text: In a 6-generation family, Mirzaa et al. (2025) used exome sequencing to identify a hemizygous c.271C-T transition in the SMARCA1 gene (NM_003069.4), resulting in an arg91-to-ter (R91X) substitution. It was found in a proband, his brother, and 2 maternal cousins, who had intellectual disability or learning disability and macrocephaly (OFC +4.3 to +6 SD). Other features in the family included hydrocephalus, hepatosplenomegaly, overgrowth, and obesity. Both mothers carried the variant and had only mildly increased head circumference and no reported learning disability. The paternal grandfather and a maternal uncle did not carry the variant. The same variant was maternally inherited in a second, unrelated family, in a 6-year-old boy with macrocephaly, ASD, and ADHD.

paragraphs.text: Mirzaa et al. (2025) identified a maternally inherited c.757C-T transition in the SMARCA1 gene, resulting in an arg253-to-ter (R253X) substitution, in a family (family 9) with 2 affected sibs: - A 4-year-4-month-old boy had an OFC of +5.9 SD, mild intellectual disability, and tall stature. - His 7-year-4-month-old sister had an OFC of -0.4 SD and was much more severely affected, with severe vision problems, feeding difficulties, laryngeal palsy, and facial palsy. - Their mother, an obligate carrier, had an OFC of +5.6 SD, mild learning disability, and tall stature. When expressed in U2OS cells, the variant produced a stable truncated 35-kD protein at a somewhat lower level than the other variants tested. This protein was found in the cytoplasm as well as the nucleus.
